claim: The budding yeast Cdc13, Stn1 and Ten1 proteins form a heterotrimeric complex.
source: The budding yeast Cdc13, Stn1 and Ten1 proteins form a heterotrimeric complex, and the inactivation of any of its subunits leads to a uniformly lethal phenotype due to telomere deprotection.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the CST complex in budding yeast, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: The inactivation of any CST subunit leads to a uniformly lethal phenotype due to telomere deprotection.
source: The budding yeast Cdc13, Stn1 and Ten1 proteins form a heterotrimeric complex, and the inactivation of any of its subunits leads to a uniformly lethal phenotype due to telomere deprotection.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the CST complex in budding yeast, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: The deletion of CDC13 in SY14 leads to telomere erosion and intrachromosome end-to-end fusion.
source: Here, we employed the single-linear-chromosome yeast SY14, and surprisingly found that the deletion of CDC13 leads to telomere erosion and intrachromosome end-to-end fusion, which depends on Rad52 but not Yku.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including Southern blotting, PCR mapping, and sequencing results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Chromosome end-to-end fusion in SY14 cdc13Δ depends on Rad52 but not Yku.
source: Here, we employed the single-linear-chromosome yeast SY14, and surprisingly found that the deletion of CDC13 leads to telomere erosion and intrachromosome end-to-end fusion, which depends on Rad52 but not Yku.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that deletion of RAD52 reduces fusion efficiency by over 60-fold, while deletion of YKU70 has no significant effect (Figure 4C).

claim: The emergence frequency of survivors in the SY14 cdc13Δ mutant was ~29 fold higher than that in either the stn1Δ or ten1Δ mutant.
source: Interestingly, the emergence frequency of survivors in the SY14 cdc13Δ mutant was ~29 fold higher than that in either the stn1Δ or ten1Δ mutant, demonstrating a predominant role of Cdc13 in inhibiting telomere fusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative survivor formation assays shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cdc13 plays a predominant role in inhibiting telomere fusion.
source: Interestingly, the emergence frequency of survivors in the SY14 cdc13Δ mutant was ~29 fold higher than that in either the stn1Δ or ten1Δ mutant, demonstrating a predominant role of Cdc13 in inhibiting telomere fusion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing differential survivor frequencies in different CST deletion mutants.

claim: Chromosomal fusion readily occurred in the telomerase-null SY14 strain.
source: Chromosomal fusion readily occurred in the telomerase-null SY14 strain, further verifying the default role of intact telomeres in inhibiting chromosome fusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6, showing chromosome fusion in SY14 tlc1Δ cells.

claim: Intact telomeres play a default role in inhibiting chromosome fusion.
source: Chromosomal fusion readily occurred in the telomerase-null SY14 strain, further verifying the default role of intact telomeres in inhibiting chromosome fusion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that loss of telomerase leads to chromosome fusion.

claim: Telomere length in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is approximately 300 ± 75 bp.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, telomere length is approximately 300 ± 75 bp, comprising double-stranded TG1-3/C1-3A repeats and a 12–14 nt-long G-rich single-stranded tail (Larrivée et al., 2004; Wellinger et al., 1993; Zakian, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Larrivée et al., 2004; Wellinger et al., 1993; Zakian, 1996).

claim: Yeast telomeres comprise double-stranded TG1-3/C1-3A repeats and a 12–14 nt-long G-rich single-stranded tail.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, telomere length is approximately 300 ± 75 bp, comprising double-stranded TG1-3/C1-3A repeats and a 12–14 nt-long G-rich single-stranded tail (Larrivée et al., 2004; Wellinger et al., 1993; Zakian, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Larrivée et al., 2004; Wellinger et al., 1993; Zakian, 1996).

claim: Y′ elements are located immediately internal to telomeric DNA and are present in zero to four tandem copies.
source: Y′ elements, located immediately internal to telomeric DNA, are present in zero to four tandem copies and fall into two classes, Y′ long (6.7 kb) and Y′ short (5.2 kb).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about yeast telomere structure.

claim: Y′ elements fall into two classes: Y′ long (6.7 kb) and Y′ short (5.2 kb).
source: Y′ elements, located immediately internal to telomeric DNA, are present in zero to four tandem copies and fall into two classes, Y′ long (6.7 kb) and Y′ short (5.2 kb).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about yeast telomere structure.

claim: Y′ elements exhibit at least 98% identity, even between different strains.
source: Y′ elements exhibit homogeneity, showing at least 98% identity, even between different strains (Chan and Tye, 1983a; Chan and Tye, 1983b; Louis and Haber, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Chan and Tye, 1983a; Chan and Tye, 1983b; Louis and Haber, 1992).

claim: X elements are located centromere-proximal to telomeres or Y′ elements and are less conserved than Y′ elements.
source: In contrast, X elements, which are located centromere-proximal to telomeres or Y′ elements, are less conserved, with 8–18% divergence occurring between various X elements, and they are found in virtually all telomeres (Louis and Haber, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Louis and Haber, 1991).

claim: X elements show 8–18% divergence between various X elements.
source: In contrast, X elements, which are located centromere-proximal to telomeres or Y′ elements, are less conserved, with 8–18% divergence occurring between various X elements, and they are found in virtually all telomeres (Louis and Haber, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Louis and Haber, 1991).

claim: X elements are found in virtually all telomeres.
source: In contrast, X elements, which are located centromere-proximal to telomeres or Y′ elements, are less conserved, with 8–18% divergence occurring between various X elements, and they are found in virtually all telomeres (Louis and Haber, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Louis and Haber, 1991).

claim: Telomeres progressively shorten at a rate of 3–5 nt per cell division in yeast in the absence of telomerase.
source: Because of the end-replication problem observed in the vast majority of eukaryotic cells (Olovnikov, 1971; Watson, 1972), telomeres progressively shorten at a rate of 3–5 nt per cell division in yeast, leading to chromosome end erosions in the absence of telomerase (Lendvay et al., 1996; Lingner, 1997b; Marcand et al., 1999; Singer and Gottschling, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lendvay et al., 1996; Lingner, 1997b; Marcand et al., 1999; Singer and Gottschling, 1994).

claim: Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein complex consisting of Est2, Tlc1, Est1, Est3, and Pop1/Pop6/Pop7 proteins.
source: Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein complex consisting of the catalytic subunit Est2, the RNA moiety Tlc1, accessory factors Est1 and Est3 and the Pop1/Pop6/Pop7 proteins (Lemieux et al., 2016; Lendvay et al., 1996; Lundblad and Szostak, 1989; Singer and Gottschling, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lemieux et al., 2016; Lendvay et al., 1996; Lundblad and Szostak, 1989; Singer and Gottschling, 1994).

claim: The core telomerase complex formed by Est2 and Tlc1 is sufficient to catalyze telomere addition in vitro.
source: Although the deletion of either EST1 or EST3 leads to a defect in telomerase function in vivo, the core telomerase complex formed by the reverse transcriptase Est2 and the RNA template Tlc1 is sufficient to catalyze telomere addition in vitro (Liao et al., 2005; Lingner et al., 1997a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Liao et al., 2005; Lingner et al., 1997a).

claim: Est1 recruits telomerase to telomeres through its interaction with Cdc13.
source: Est1 recruits telomerase to telomeres through its interaction with the ssDNA-binding protein Cdc13.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about telomerase recruitment.

claim: Est1 promotes G-quadruplex formation to stimulate telomerase activity and provide telomere protection.
source: Additionally, it promotes G-quadruplex formation to stimulate telomerase activity and provide telomere protection (Tong et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Tong et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2010).

claim: Est3 has been suggested to activate telomerase.
source: The function of Est3 is less clear, and it has been suggested to activate telomerase (Talley et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Talley et al., 2011).

claim: Most cells lacking telomerase undergo senescence after 50–100 rounds of cell division.
source: Although most of the cells lacking telomerase undergo senescence after 50–100 rounds of cell division, a few cells can maintain their telomeres via recombination-dependent mechanisms, yielding two types of survivors, referred to as Type I and Type II.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about telomerase-null cells.

claim: A few telomerase-null cells can maintain their telomeres via recombination-dependent mechanisms, yielding Type I and Type II survivors.
source: Although most of the cells lacking telomerase undergo senescence after 50–100 rounds of cell division, a few cells can maintain their telomeres via recombination-dependent mechanisms, yielding two types of survivors, referred to as Type I and Type II.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about telomerase-null cells.

claim: Type I survivors exhibit massive amplification of subtelomeric Y′ sequences with very short TG1–3 repeats at the ends.
source: Type I survivors exhibit massive amplification of subtelomeric Y′ sequences with very short TG1–3 repeats at the ends, while Type II survivors amplify TG1-3 repeats and display a heterogeneous pattern of long terminal TG1–3 tracts (Lundblad and Blackburn, 1993; Teng and Zakian, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lundblad and Blackburn, 1993; Teng and Zakian, 1999).

claim: Type II survivors amplify TG1-3 repeats and display a heterogeneous pattern of long terminal TG1–3 tracts.
source: Type I survivors exhibit massive amplification of subtelomeric Y′ sequences with very short TG1–3 repeats at the ends, while Type II survivors amplify TG1-3 repeats and display a heterogeneous pattern of long terminal TG1–3 tracts (Lundblad and Blackburn, 1993; Teng and Zakian, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Lundblad and Blackburn, 1993; Teng and Zakian, 1999).

claim: The formation of Type I and Type II survivors relies on the RAD51 and RAD50 gene epistasis groups, respectively.
source: The formation of Type I and Type II survivors relies on the RAD51 and RAD50 gene epistasis groups, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about survivor formation pathways.

claim: The deletion of both RAD50 and RAD51 almost eliminates survivor generation, as observed in rad52Δ mutants.
source: Thus, the deletion of both RAD50 and RAD51 almost eliminates survivor generation, as observed in rad52Δ mutants (Chen et al., 2001; Le et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Chen et al., 2001; Le et al., 1999).

claim: The double-stranded TG1-3 repeats are bound by Rap1.
source: In budding yeast, the double-stranded TG1-3 repeats and the G tail are bound by an array of Rap1 and Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 (CST) complexes, respectively (Bourns et al., 1998; Gilson et al., 1993; Hughes et al., 2000; Lin and Zakian, 1996; Nugent et al., 1996; Price et al., 2010; Ray and Runge, 1999; Tsukamoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bourns et al., 1998; Gilson et al., 1993; Hughes et al., 2000; Lin and Zakian, 1996; Nugent et al., 1996; Price et al., 2010; Ray and Runge, 1999; Tsukamoto et al., 2001).

claim: The G tail is bound by the Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 (CST) complex.
source: In budding yeast, the double-stranded TG1-3 repeats and the G tail are bound by an array of Rap1 and Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 (CST) complexes, respectively (Bourns et al., 1998; Gilson et al., 1993; Hughes et al., 2000; Lin and Zakian, 1996; Nugent et al., 1996; Price et al., 2010; Ray and Runge, 1999; Tsukamoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bourns et al., 1998; Gilson et al., 1993; Hughes et al., 2000; Lin and Zakian, 1996; Nugent et al., 1996; Price et al., 2010; Ray and Runge, 1999; Tsukamoto et al., 2001).

claim: Rap1 is required for cell viability.
source: Rap1 is required for cell viability and performs many distinct essential cellular tasks, such as transcription regulation and telomere protection (Buck and Lieb, 2006; Diffley, 1992; Lieb et al., 2001; Pardo and Marcand, 2005; Shore, 1994; Shore and Nasmyth, 1987; Tomar et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Buck and Lieb, 2006; Diffley, 1992; Lieb et al., 2001; Pardo and Marcand, 2005; Shore, 1994; Shore and Nasmyth, 1987; Tomar et al., 2008).

claim: Rap1 performs many distinct essential cellular tasks, such as transcription regulation and telomere protection.
source: Rap1 is required for cell viability and performs many distinct essential cellular tasks, such as transcription regulation and telomere protection (Buck and Lieb, 2006; Diffley, 1992; Lieb et al., 2001; Pardo and Marcand, 2005; Shore, 1994; Shore and Nasmyth, 1987; Tomar et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Buck and Lieb, 2006; Diffley, 1992; Lieb et al., 2001; Pardo and Marcand, 2005; Shore, 1994; Shore and Nasmyth, 1987; Tomar et al., 2008).

claim: The CST complex specifically binds telomeric single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and acts as a telomere-capping protein and telomerase regulator.
source: The CST complex specifically binds telomeric single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and acts as a telomere-capping protein and telomerase regulator.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the CST complex.

claim: The CST complex structurally resembles heterotrimeric replication protein A (RPA).
source: This trimeric complex structurally resembles heterotrimeric replication protein A (RPA), a eukaryotic major ssDNA-binding protein, indicating that the CST complex may function as a specialized telomere-dedicated RPA-like complex (Gao et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Gao et al., 2007).

claim: Cdc13 plays dual roles in telomere protection and telomerase recruitment.
source: Cdc13, the major single-stranded telomere-binding protein, plays dual roles in telomere protection and telomerase recruitment (Bourns et al., 1998; Hughes et al., 2000; Lin and Zakian, 1996; Nugent et al., 1996; Tsukamoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Bourns et al., 1998; Hughes et al., 2000; Lin and Zakian, 1996; Nugent et al., 1996; Tsukamoto et al., 2001).

claim: Cdc13 interacts with Est1 and regulates telomerase access to telomeres in late S phase.
source: Cdc13 interacts with Est1 and regulates telomerase access to telomeres in late S phase (Chen et al., 2018; Evans and Lundblad, 1999; Osterhage et al., 2006; Pennock et al., 2001; Qi and Zakian, 2000; Taggart et al., 2002; Wu and Zakian, 2011), after which G-rich strand extension is limited by Stn1, whose binding site partially overlaps with that of Est1 (Chandra et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Chen et al., 2018; Evans and Lundblad, 1999; Osterhage et al., 2006; Pennock et al., 2001; Qi and Zakian, 2000; Taggart et al., 2002; Wu and Zakian, 2011).

claim: G-rich strand extension is limited by Stn1, whose binding site partially overlaps with that of Est1.
source: Cdc13 interacts with Est1 and regulates telomerase access to telomeres in late S phase (Chen et al., 2018; Evans and Lundblad, 1999; Osterhage et al., 2006; Pennock et al., 2001; Qi and Zakian, 2000; Taggart et al., 2002; Wu and Zakian, 2011), after which G-rich strand extension is limited by Stn1, whose binding site partially overlaps with that of Est1 (Chandra et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Chandra et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2000).

claim: Stn1 and Ten1 subunits are recruited to telomere ends via direct interaction with Cdc13.
source: The Stn1 and Ten1 subunits are recruited to telomere ends via direct interaction with Cdc13.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about CST complex assembly.

claim: Both Stn1 and Ten1 display a relatively weak telomeric DNA binding affinity.
source: Both Stn1 and Ten1 are reported to display a relatively weak telomeric DNA binding affinity and to exhibit Cdc13-independent functions (Gao et al., 2007; Qian et al., 2010; Qian et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Gao et al., 2007; Qian et al., 2010; Qian et al., 2009).

claim: Stn1 and Ten1 exhibit Cdc13-independent functions.
source: Both Stn1 and Ten1 are reported to display a relatively weak telomeric DNA binding affinity and to exhibit Cdc13-independent functions (Gao et al., 2007; Qian et al., 2010; Qian et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Gao et al., 2007; Qian et al., 2010; Qian et al., 2009).

claim: The amino terminus of Stn1 is sufficient for Ten1 binding.
source: The amino terminus of Stn1 is sufficient for Ten1 binding, while its carboxyl terminus interacts with both Cdc13 and Pol12 (a subunit of the DNA Polα complex) (Grossi et al., 2004; Petreaca et al., 2006; Puglisi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Grossi et al., 2004; Petreaca et al., 2006; Puglisi et al., 2008).

claim: The carboxyl terminus of Stn1 interacts with both Cdc13 and Pol12.
source: The amino terminus of Stn1 is sufficient for Ten1 binding, while its carboxyl terminus interacts with both Cdc13 and Pol12 (a subunit of the DNA Polα complex) (Grossi et al., 2004; Petreaca et al., 2006; Puglisi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Grossi et al., 2004; Petreaca et al., 2006; Puglisi et al., 2008).

claim: Stn1 promotes the recruitment of Polα for lagging strand DNA replication.
source: In addition to limiting G-rich strand extension, Stn1 promotes the recruitment of Polα for lagging strand DNA replication (Grossi et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Grossi et al., 2004).

claim: Stn1 is the primary effector of telomere capping.
source: Notably, many lines of evidence support the notion that Stn1 is the primary effector of telomere capping.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence cited in the manuscript.

claim: Fusing the DNA-binding domain of Cdc13 to Stn1 is sufficient to bypass the essential function of Cdc13.
source: For instance, either fusing the DNA-binding domain of Cdc13 to Stn1 or cooverexpressing Ten1 with a truncated form of Stn1 is sufficient to bypass the essential function of Cdc13 (Pennock et al., 2001; Petreaca et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Pennock et al., 2001; Petreaca et al., 2006).

claim: Cooverexpressing Ten1 with a truncated form of Stn1 is sufficient to bypass the essential function of Cdc13.
source: For instance, either fusing the DNA-binding domain of Cdc13 to Stn1 or cooverexpressing Ten1 with a truncated form of Stn1 is sufficient to bypass the essential function of Cdc13 (Pennock et al., 2001; Petreaca et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Pennock et al., 2001; Petreaca et al., 2006).

claim: Ten1 appears to promote the activity of Cdc13.
source: Although Ten1 remains less well characterized, it appears to promote the activity of Cdc13 (Qian et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Qian et al., 2009).

claim: Cdc13, Stn1 and Ten1 are all required for cell viability and telomere length regulation.
source: Nevertheless, Cdc13, Stn1 and Ten1 are all required for cell viability and telomere length regulation.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the CST complex.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in each CST subunit result in the accumulation of telomeric ssDNA and abnormal elongation of telomeres.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in each subunit result in the accumulation of telomeric ssDNA and abnormal elongation of telomeres (Garvik et al., 1995; Grandin et al., 2001b; Grandin et al., 1997), suggesting that Cdc13, Stn1 and Ten1 are epistatic in telomere protection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Garvik et al., 1995; Grandin et al., 2001b; Grandin et al., 1997).

claim: Mammalian CST (CTC1-STN1-TEN1) appears to have extratelomeric functions in DNA replication.
source: Mammalian CST (CTC1-STN1-TEN1) appears to have extratelomeric functions in DNA replication (Price et al., 2010; Stewart et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Price et al., 2010; Stewart et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019).

claim: The overexpression of Stn1 results in its mislocalization to a nontelomeric region where it interferes with replication fork integrity.
source: One clue concerning this question comes from the observation that the overexpression of Stn1 results in its mislocalization to a nontelomeric region where it interferes with replication fork integrity (Gasparyan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Gasparyan et al., 2009).

claim: Single-chromosome yeast strains SY14 and SY15 were created via CRISPR-Cas9 method.
source: We recently successively fused the 16 chromosomes of budding yeast via a CRISPR-Cas9 method (Shao et al., 2019b) and created single-chromosome yeast strains, designated SY14 and SY15, which contain a single linear or circular chromosome, respectively (Shao et al., 2019a; Shao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors (Shao et al., 2019b; Shao et al., 2019a; Shao et al., 2018).

claim: SY14 contains a single linear chromosome.
source: We recently successively fused the 16 chromosomes of budding yeast via a CRISPR-Cas9 method (Shao et al., 2019b) and created single-chromosome yeast strains, designated SY14 and SY15, which contain a single linear or circular chromosome, respectively (Shao et al., 2019a; Shao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors (Shao et al., 2019b; Shao et al., 2019a; Shao et al., 2018).

claim: SY15 contains a single circular chromosome.
source: We recently successively fused the 16 chromosomes of budding yeast via a CRISPR-Cas9 method (Shao et al., 2019b) and created single-chromosome yeast strains, designated SY14 and SY15, which contain a single linear or circular chromosome, respectively (Shao et al., 2019a; Shao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors (Shao et al., 2019b; Shao et al., 2019a; Shao et al., 2018).

claim: The progeny colonies of SY14 and SY15 obtained after various re-streaks displayed the same size as the parental colonies.
source: The progeny colonies obtained after various re-streaks displayed the same size as the parental colonies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The growth rates of the subclones in liquid YPD medium were nearly identical to those of the original clones.
source: The growth rates of the subclones in liquid YPD medium were nearly identical to those of the original clones (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The single chromosome in SY14 remained intact during the passages.
source: In addition, a pulse-field-gel electrophoresis (PFG) analysis revealed that the single chromosome in SY14 remained intact during the passages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The telomere restriction fragment (TRF) in SY14 was maintained at a relatively stable length (~1.3 ± 0.1 kb) during successive passages.
source: Moreover, telomere Southern blotting assay showed that in all successively passaged clones, the telomere restriction fragment (TRF) was maintained at a relatively stable length (~1.3 ± 0.1 kb), comparable to that in the parental clone (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Rap1 is indispensable for the viability of the circular-chromosome yeast SY15.
source: The results showed that Rap1 was indispensable for the viability of the circular-chromosome yeast SY15 (Figure 2A), suggesting that Rap1 is essential not only for telomere protection but also for gene transcription, consistent with a previous report that the telomere binding of Rap1 is not required for its essential functions (Alexander and Zakian, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The lack of CDC13, STN1 or TEN1 led to the death of SY14 cells but did not affect the viability of the SY15 strain.
source: In contrast, the lack of CDC13, STN1 or TEN1 led to the death of SY14 cells but did not affect the viability (Figure 2B) or the growth rate (Figure 2C) of the SY15 strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The lethality of CST depletion is mainly caused by defects in telomere protection.
source: These data indicate that the lethality of CST depletion is mainly caused by defects in telomere protection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that CST deletion is lethal in SY14 but not SY15.

claim: The interstitial telomeric sequences (ITSs) of TG255/CA255 were successfully transmitted from generation to generation in all the SY15CA255 and SY15TG255 strains, regardless of the presence or absence of CST.
source: The interstitial telomeric sequences (ITSs) of TG255/CA255 determined by Southern blotting were successfully transmitted from generation to generation in all the SY15CA255 and SY15TG255 strains, regardless of the presence or absence of CST (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There were no mutations in ITSs after ~100 population doublings in cst mutants.
source: Further sequencing results for three independent clones of each cst mutant confirmed that there were no mutations after ~100 population doublings (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The CST complex does not affect the replication of ITSs.
source: These results suggest that the CST complex does not affect the replication of ITSs; that is, the CST complex might have no function in telomere replication other than the recruitment of Polα for lagging strand synthesis (Grossi et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing stable transmission of ITSs in CST mutants.

claim: Approximately 1‰ of SY14 cdc13Δ cells survived through Rad52-mediated chromosomal end-to-end fusion.
source: Unexpectedly, approximately 1‰ of these cells survived through Rad52-mediated chromosomal end-to-end fusion (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Y′-telomere band of ~1.3 kb was not detected in the majority of SY14 cdc13Δ survivors.
source: Notably, the Y′-telomere band of ~1.3 kb was not detected, while an ~15 kb band emerged in the majority of cells (27 out of 30) (Figure 3A), suggesting that the telomere structure of SY14 cdc13Δ survivors is totally different from that of SY14 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: An ~15 kb band emerged in the majority of SY14 cdc13Δ survivors (27 out of 30).
source: Notably, the Y′-telomere band of ~1.3 kb was not detected, while an ~15 kb band emerged in the majority of cells (27 out of 30) (Figure 3A), suggesting that the telomere structure of SY14 cdc13Δ survivors is totally different from that of SY14 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In most SY14 cdc13Δ survived clones, fusion took place in the telomeric 5′-TG1-3-3′ region of Chr XVI-L and the distal '5′-(CA)17-3′' region located 43.9 kb away from the telomeric TG1-3 sequence of Chr X-R.
source: Notably, in most survived clones, fusion took place in the telomeric 5′-TG1-3-3′ region of Chr XVI-L and the distal '5′-(CA)17-3′' region, which is located 43.9 kb away from the telomeric TG1-3 sequence of Chr X-R (e.g., SY14 cdc13Δ−30, Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including sequencing results shown in Figure 4A and Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The retained TG1-3 sequences of Chr XVI-L in individual circular chromosomes ranged from 21 to 374 bp long, with an average length of 126 bp.
source: The retained TG1-3 sequences of Chr XVI-L in individual circular chromosomes were of different lengths: ranging from 21 to 374 bp long, with an average length of 126 bp (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The efficiency of chromosomal fusion in the SY14 cdc13Δ rad52Δ strain was over 60-fold lower than that in the SY14 cdc13Δ strain.
source: The results revealed that the efficiency of chromosomal fusion in the SY14 cdc13Δ rad52Δ strain was over 60-fold lower than that in the SY14 cdc13Δ strain (Figure 4C), indicating that chromosome-end fusions were mainly mediated by the Rad52 pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Chromosome-end fusions in SY14 cdc13Δ were mainly mediated by the Rad52 pathway.
source: The results revealed that the efficiency of chromosomal fusion in the SY14 cdc13Δ rad52Δ strain was over 60-fold lower than that in the SY14 cdc13Δ strain (Figure 4C), indicating that chromosome-end fusions were mainly mediated by the Rad52 pathway.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the effect of RAD52 deletion on fusion efficiency.

claim: The efficiency of chromosomal fusion in the SY14 cdc13Δ yku70Δ strain was comparable to that in the SY14 cdc13Δ strain.
source: In contrast, the efficiency of chromosomal fusion in the SY14 cdc13Δ yku70Δ strain was comparable to that in the SY14 cdc13Δ strain (Figure 4C), suggesting that the NHEJ pathway contributes little to chromosomal fusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The NHEJ pathway contributes little to chromosomal fusion in SY14 cdc13Δ cells.
source: In contrast, the efficiency of chromosomal fusion in the SY14 cdc13Δ yku70Δ strain was comparable to that in the SY14 cdc13Δ strain (Figure 4C), suggesting that the NHEJ pathway contributes little to chromosomal fusion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that YKU70 deletion does not affect fusion efficiency.

claim: The further deletion of POL32 in the cdc13∆ mutant resulted in an approximately 3-fold decrease in chromosome fusion rates compared to the single deletion of CDC13.
source: The quantitative survivor formation assay showed that the further deletion of POL32 in the cdc13∆ mutant resulted in an approximately 3-fold decrease in chromosome fusion rates compared to the single deletion of CDC13 (Figure 4E), indicating that chromosomal circularization in SY14 cdc13Δ survivors partially depends on Pol32.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Chromosomal circularization in SY14 cdc13Δ survivors partially depends on Pol32.
source: The quantitative survivor formation assay showed that the further deletion of POL32 in the cdc13∆ mutant resulted in an approximately 3-fold decrease in chromosome fusion rates compared to the single deletion of CDC13 (Figure 4E), indicating that chromosomal circularization in SY14 cdc13Δ survivors partially depends on Pol32.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the effect of POL32 deletion on fusion rates.

claim: The frequency of intrachromosomal fusion in the SY14 stn1∆ and SY14 ten1∆ strains was 0.04‰.
source: The results showed that the frequency of intrachromosomal fusion in the SY14 stn1∆ and SY14 ten1∆ strains was 0.04‰, which was ~29 fold lower than the 1.14‰ frequency observed in the cdc13∆ strain (Figure 5A), indicating that Cdc13, Stn1 and Ten1 play nonequivalent roles in telomere capping: Cdc13 plays a much more dominant role than Stn1 and Ten1 in inhibiting chromosome end fusions (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The further deletion of CDC13 in stn1∆ and ten1∆ mutants resulted in approximately 10- and 6-fold increases in chromosome fusion rates compared to the single deletion of STN1 or TEN1, respectively.
source: Thus, we quantified the chromosome fusion frequency in cdc13∆ stn1∆ and cdc13∆ ten1∆ double mutants and found that the further deletion of CDC13 in stn1∆ and ten1∆ mutants resulted in approximately 10- and 6-fold increases in chromosome fusion rates compared to the single deletion of STN1 or TEN1, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The percentage of rTG Type chromosome fusion in cdc13∆ stn1∆ and cdc13∆ ten1∆ double mutants was 86% and 89%, respectively.
source: Further detailed mapping (Figure 5—figure supplement 4) and characterization (Figure 5—figure supplement 5) of chromosome fusions revealed that the increase in chromosome fusion in cdc13∆ stn1∆ and cdc13∆ ten1∆ double mutants was likely attributed to the elevation of the percentage of rTG Type chromosome fusion, which was 86% and 89% in the cdc13∆ stn1∆ and cdc13∆ ten1∆ mutants, respectively (Figure 5D), comparable to the 92% rate in SY14 cdc13Δ cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Independent of Cdc13, Stn1 and Ten1 play roles in inhibiting chromosome fusion.
source: Interestingly, the chromosome fusion rates in the cdc13∆ stn1∆ and cdc13∆ ten1∆ strains were significantly lower than those in the cdc13∆ strain, suggesting that independent of Cdc13, Stn1 and Ten1 play roles in inhibiting chromosome fusion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that double mutants have lower fusion rates than cdc13Δ alone.

claim: All clones of SY14CA255 cstΔ survivors were of the rTG Type and utilized CA255 instead of the '5′-(CA)17-3′' repeat sequence at their fusion junctions.
source: The results revealed that all of the clones were of the rTG Type and utilized CA255 instead of the '5′-(CA)17-3′' repeat sequence at their fusion junctions (Figure 5—figure supplement 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6E.

claim: Chromosome circularization preferentially occurred at sites where complementary sequences existed on two telomeres.
source: Therefore, chromosome circularization preferentially occurred at sites where complementary sequences existed on two telomeres.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing preferential use of inserted CA255 sequences.

claim: The telomeres of SY14 tlc1Δ cells shortened with increasing passages and reached a critical length at different time points when the cells were in the senescent state.
source: Southern blotting assay revealed that the telomeres of SY14 tlc1Δ cells shortened with increasing passages and reached a critical length at different time points when the cells were in the senescent state (Figure 6B), which is an indication of a correlation between telomere erosion and cellular senescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Among three individual SY14 tlc1Δ clones, two generated Type II survivors with the amplification of TG repeats, while one exhibited a pattern similar to that of SY14 cdc13Δ cells.
source: Among three individual clones, two (clones 1 and 3) generated Type II survivors with the amplification of TG repeats, while one (clone 2) exhibited a pattern that was totally different from that of either Type I or Type II survivors but was similar to that of SY14 cdc13Δ cells (Figures 3A and 6B), suggesting that chromosome fusion had taken place.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The SY14 tlc1Δ cells senesced at the 3rd re-streak (~75 generations) on plates.
source: In solid medium, the SY14 tlc1Δ cells senesced at the 3rd re-streak (~75 generations) on plates (Figure 6C), and survivors gradually emerged thereafter.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Most of the survived SY14 tlc1Δ cells had experienced chromosomal circularization via homologous TG1-3/C1-3A DNA sequences.
source: Further erosion-border mapping (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), fusion type assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) and fusion junction sequencing (Figure 6—figure supplements 2B and 3) confirmed that most of the survived SY14 tlc1Δ cells had experienced chromosomal circularization via homologous TG1-3/C1-3A DNA sequences, as seen in SY14 cdc13Δ survivors, which could be perpetually maintained under laboratory conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1, 2, and 3.

claim: In the rTG Type circular chromosome of SY14 tlc1Δ cells, the retained TG1-3/C1-3A sequences at junction points were 18 to 58 bp long (36 bp long on average).
source: Notably, in the rTG Type circular chromosome of SY14 tlc1Δ cells, the retained TG1-3/C1-3A sequences at junction points were 18 to 58 bp long (36 bp long on average) (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), which was much shorter than those in SY14 cdc13Δ survivors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: In SY14 tlc1Δ cells, chromosome fusion takes place passively after telomeres have experienced extensive shortening (crisis).
source: We propose that in SY14 tlc1Δ cells, chromosome fusion takes place passively after telomeres have experienced extensive shortening (crisis), while in SY14 cdc13Δ cells, chromosome fusion occurs immediately upon telomere deprotection via the loss of Cdc13.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of retained TG sequences in tlc1Δ versus cdc13Δ survivors.

claim: In SY14 cdc13Δ cells, chromosome fusion occurs immediately upon telomere deprotection via the loss of Cdc13.
source: We propose that in SY14 tlc1Δ cells, chromosome fusion takes place passively after telomeres have experienced extensive shortening (crisis), while in SY14 cdc13Δ cells, chromosome fusion occurs immediately upon telomere deprotection via the loss of Cdc13.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of retained TG sequences in tlc1Δ versus cdc13Δ survivors.

claim: With the reduction in chromosome numbers, the frequency of Type II survivor emergence gradually decreased, while Y' recombination was readily detected, indicating an increase of Type I survivors.
source: With the reduction in chromosome numbers, the frequency of Type II survivor emergence gradually decreased, while Y' recombination was readily detected, indicating an increase of Type I survivors (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B-Ε).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B-E.

claim: The efficiency of telomere recombination is affected by chromosomal numbers in budding yeast.
source: These data suggest that the efficiency of telomere recombination is affected by chromosomal numbers in budding yeast.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing changes in survivor types with chromosome number.

claim: In yeast strains with eight or fewer chromosomes, chromosome fusions might exist.
source: Notably, some distinct bands (indicated by open arrows on the right in the panels) with a size larger or smaller than the Y'-element occasionally emerged in SY7 tlc1Δ clones (eight chromosomes) as well as in SY tlc1Δ clones with fewer chromosomes, suggesting that in yeast strains with eight or fewer chromosomes, chromosome fusions might exist.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing distinct bands in strains with fewer chromosomes.

claim: The double deletion of TLC1 and RAD52 in the SY14 strain accelerated senescence.
source: The results showed that the double deletion of TLC1 and RAD52 in the SY14 strain accelerated senescence (Figure 7A), and SY14 tlc1Δ rad52Δ survivors eventually appeared but seemed to be much more difficult to obtain than SY14 tlc1Δ survivors (Figure 7A), suggesting that Rad52 plays an important role in survivor generation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Rad52 plays an important role in survivor generation in SY14 tlc1Δ cells.
source: The results showed that the double deletion of TLC1 and RAD52 in the SY14 strain accelerated senescence (Figure 7A), and SY14 tlc1Δ rad52Δ survivors eventually appeared but seemed to be much more difficult to obtain than SY14 tlc1Δ survivors (Figure 7A), suggesting that Rad52 plays an important role in survivor generation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing difficulty in obtaining survivors in the double mutant.

claim: No rTG Type survivors were generated in SY14 tlc1Δ rad52Δ cells.
source: Further chromosome fusion mapping and sequencing results showed that no rTG Type survivors were generated in SY14 tlc1Δ rad52Δ cells (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: The rTG Type survivor generation rate in SY14 tlc1Δ yku70Δ was 81%, comparable to 84% in SY14 tlc1Δ cells.
source: The SY14 tlc1Δ yku70Δ survivor types were also examined (Figure 7—figure supplement 4), and the rTG Type survivor generation rate was 81%, comparable to 84% in SY14 tlc1Δ cells (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The RAD52 pathway plays a dominant role in chromosomal end-to-end fusion in SY14 tlc1Δ cells.
source: These data indicate that the RAD52 pathway plays a dominant role in chromosomal end-to-end fusion in SY14 tlc1Δ cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the effects of RAD52 and YKU70 deletions on survivor types.

claim: The deletion of POL32 in the SY14 tlc1Δ strain did not affect the development of survivors.
source: Both SY14 tlc1Δ and SY14 tlc1Δ pol32Δ cells senesced at the 3rd re-streak on plates, and survivors gradually emerged at the 7th re-streak (Figure 7D), suggesting that the deletion of POL32 in the SY14 tlc1Δ strain did not affect the development of survivors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The rTG Type survivor rate in SY14 tlc1Δ pol32Δ cells was 100%, which was higher than the 84% rate observed in SY14 tlc1Δ cells.
source: Further chromosome fusion mapping (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A and B) and fusion type assay (Figure 7—figure supplement 5C) revealed that the rTG Type survivor rate in SY14 tlc1Δ pol32Δ cells was 100%, which was higher than the 84% rate observed in SY14 tlc1Δ cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Pol32 is not required for the generation of rTG Type survivors but might function in non-TG Type development in SY14 tlc1Δ cells.
source: These data suggest that Pol32 is not required for the generation of rTG Type survivors but might function in non-TG Type development in SY14 tlc1Δ cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the effect of POL32 deletion on survivor types.

claim: The essentiality of CST is attributed to its roles in telomere protection.
source: In SY15 cells containing a single circular chromosome, the deletion of CDC13, STN1 or TEN1 does not appear to affect cell growth or viability (Figure 2B and C), indicating that the essentiality of CST is mainly due to telomere protection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that CST deletion is lethal in SY14 but not SY15.

claim: It is Cdc13, and not Stn1 or Ten1, that plays the major role in inhibiting chromosomal end-to-end fusion.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that it is Cdc13, and not Stn1 or Ten1, that plays the major role in inhibiting chromosomal end-to-end fusion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing differential survivor frequencies in different CST deletion mutants.

claim: rTG Type and non-TG Type chromosomal fusion are mainly achieved through the SSA pathway.
source: Given that telomere deprotection in SY14 cst∆ and SY14 tlc1∆ cells involves end resection and homologous sequence pairing (Figure 4A and B; Figure 3—figure supplements 2–4; Figure 4—figure supplement 3; Figure 5—figure supplements 3 and 5; Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3), we favor the model in which rTG Type and non-TG Type chromosomal fusions are mainly achieved through the SSA pathway.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the characteristics of the fusion events observed.

claim: Chromosomal circularization may occur via the MMEJ or BIR pathway.
source: However, we cannot rule out the possibility that chromosomal circularization occurs via the MMEJ or BIR pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging alternative possibilities.

claim: Chromosome fusion in cdc13Δ cells is partially dependent on Pol32.
source: The latter model is supported by the observation that chromosome fusion in cdc13Δ cells is partially dependent on Pol32 (Figure 4E), which is involved in both MMEJ and BIR pathways (Lee and Lee, 2007; Lydeard et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and citations to previous studies (Lee and Lee, 2007; Lydeard et al., 2007).
